title: Massachusetts 7-day opiate supply limit for an adult's first outpatient prescription and for a minor
subtopic: Adult first outpatient and minor opiate supply limit
rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a), when issuing a prescription for an opiate to an adult patient for outpatient use for the first time, a practitioner shall not issue a prescription for more than a 7-day supply, and a practitioner shall not issue an opiate prescription to a minor for more than a 7-day supply at any time and shall discuss with the parent or guardian of the minor the risks associated with opiate use and the reasons why the prescription is necessary. Under s. 19D(b), notwithstanding subsection (a), if, in the professional medical judgment of a practitioner, more than a 7-day supply of an opiate is required to treat the adult or minor patient's acute medical condition or is necessary for the treatment of chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or for palliative care, the practitioner may issue a prescription for the quantity needed to treat such acute medical condition, chronic pain, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or pain experienced while the patient is in palliative care; the condition triggering the prescription of an opiate for more than a 7-day supply shall be documented in the patient's medical record, and the practitioner shall indicate that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate to address the medical condition. Under s. 19D(c), notwithstanding subsections (a) and (b), the section shall not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.
exam_relevance: Tests the different triggers for an adult and for a minor, the practitioner's judgment and the documentation that permit a larger supply, the exclusion of medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence, and that the section's limit is stated for the practitioner.

numeric_facts.fact: maximum opiate supply on an adult's first prescription for outpatient use and on an opiate prescription for a minor at any time
numeric_facts.conditions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D(a); a greater quantity is permitted under s. 19D(b), and under s. 19D(c) the section does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence

exceptions: Under s. 19D(b) the practitioner may issue the quantity needed where, in the practitioner's professional medical judgment, more than a 7-day supply is required to treat the adult or minor patient's acute medical condition or is necessary for the treatment of chronic pain management, pain associated with a cancer diagnosis or palliative care, with the triggering condition documented in the patient's medical record and the practitioner's indication that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate.
Under s. 19D(c) the section does not apply to medications designed for the treatment of substance abuse or opioid dependence.
common_confusions: Carrying the adult conditions of outpatient use and a first-time prescription into the minor limit, which applies at any time.

Reading the section as directed to the pharmacist, when its limit, the discussion with a minor's parent or guardian and the indication that a non-opiate alternative was not appropriate are stated for the practitioner.
Expecting the basis for a larger supply to appear on the prescription, when the statute places the documentation of the triggering condition in the patient's medical record.
Assuming the limit turns on the drug's schedule, when the statute names no schedule and speaks of an opiate.
verification_notes: Read verbatim in the current text of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D on malegislature.gov on 2026-09-14.
